title: Deep in one: Acts
for: I want to know how the church began
subtitle: Fourteen sessions through all twenty-eight chapters of Acts: from a room in Jerusalem to a rented house in Rome, and how a frightened few became a church of every nation.
intro: This track reads the Acts of the Apostles in fourteen sittings, a chapter or a few chapters at a time. Acts is the second volume of a work that begins with the Gospel of Luke, and it is the only story we have of the church's first three decades. Without it, Paul's letters would float without a setting. With it, you can watch the good news cross one boundary after another: of city, of language, of race, of religion and of empire.

Each session takes about fifteen to twenty minutes: read the chapters and their notes in plain words, then come back to one question, one thing to do and one verse to keep. Acts raises questions faithful churches answer differently, about the baptism of the Spirit, about tongues and about how a church should be ordered. The track sets out each view in the form its own holders would sign and leaves those questions open. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: Acts. The group reads a chapter or a few chapters a meeting, fourteen meetings in all. Acts is a story, and stories are easy to enjoy and easy to skim. The leader's task is to slow the group down enough to notice what Luke is showing: who crosses which line, who resists, and what the Spirit does that no one planned.

Each person reads the chapters, their notes and the session before the group meets. Some sessions cover several chapters, so encourage people to read across the week rather than all at once. The meeting reads the heart of the passage aloud and talks it over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for fourteen meetings, and keep the end time you promised. A group that wants more time can take the long sessions, such as Paul's trials in chapters 20 to 26, over two meetings. A leader doesn't need to be a scholar. A leader needs to have read the passage and its notes, and to be willing to say plainly when they don't know.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit where everyone can see each other, with the text open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. A map helps more with Acts than with almost any other book, so have the map of Paul's travels open on a screen or printed on the table from the ninth session on. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own lives stays in the room, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Fifteen minutes: one person reads the heart of the passage aloud while the others follow, then someone retells the story in a few sentences.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is in the text.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words.
Five minutes: name the next chapters and the page their session opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Acts has questions that divide faithful churches. Is the baptism of the Spirit given at conversion or later? Do tongues and prophecy continue today? Does Acts give a pattern for how churches should be ordered, or a record of how one generation managed? When the group reaches one, read the note on it together, give each view in the form its own holders would sign, and don't settle for the group what the churches have not settled.

Keep two kinds of question apart. That Jesus was raised from the dead, that he poured out his Spirit, and that the good news is for every nation is the ground every church in this book stands on. How the Spirit's gifts work now, or who should lead a congregation, divides faithful churches without dividing the faith. A group that can tell those apart can disagree on the second and still pray together on the first.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Acts is full of suffering: a sudden death, a man stoned, an apostle killed while another is freed, beatings, prison and a shipwreck. Someone in the group may hear their own loss in it, or their own unanswered prayer. When that happens, stop and listen. Thank them, don't explain their suffering for them, and don't hurry them back to the passage.

Some passages have been misused to wound people: the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira read as proof that an accident or illness is God's punishment, the healings read as blame on those who are not healed, the speeches read as contempt for the Jewish people. The notes refuse every one of those readings, and so should the group. If someone says that anyone is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, fear or guilt that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: Wait for the promise
teaching: Acts opens where Luke's Gospel ends, with the risen Jesus and a small group of friends. For forty days he speaks to them about the kingdom of God, and they ask the question they have carried all along: “Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6). He doesn't scold them. He redraws the map. They will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes, and they will be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

That sentence is the outline of the whole book. Watch for it as you read: the story begins in the city, moves into the country around it, and ends in Rome. But first there is nothing to do except wait. Jesus is taken up, two men in white say he will come back the same way, and about a hundred and twenty men and women go back to an upstairs room and pray. The church begins with people who can't make it start.

open.label: Acts 1, passage by passage
open.why: The forty days, the command to wait, the ascension and the choosing of Matthias, each explained in plain words with the hard questions they raise.

also.label: Acts in the Study Bible
also.why: Who wrote Acts and when, how it continues Luke's Gospel, the passages written as we, and how the book is built.

also.label: The book of Acts
also.why: The whole book in short pictures, so you can see where it is going before you read it a few chapters at a time.

sessions.question: The disciples wanted a kingdom restored and were given a mission instead. What do you most want from God right now, and what might he be giving you in its place?
sessions.do: Read the whole of Acts 1 aloud, then draw three circles, one inside another, and label them with the places in verse 8. Keep the drawing in your Bible for the weeks ahead.

verse.text: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

group.open: When have you had to wait for something you could do nothing to hurry?
discuss: The disciples ask about the kingdom for Israel, and Jesus answers with the ends of the earth. What does his answer keep, and what does it widen?
Why do you think Luke tells us the women and Jesus' own family were in the room praying?
The first thing the church does after the ascension is wait and pray. What would it look like for a church to begin there today?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for patience with what God has not yet done, and ask for the Spirit's help to be a witness where each of you already lives.

sessions.title: Pentecost
teaching: Pentecost was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. Jesus had died at Passover. Seven weeks later a sound like wind fills the house, flames rest on each of them, and they are all filled with the Holy Spirit and speak in other languages. The crowd hears its own tongues, from Rome to Arabia. Many readers think of Babel, where languages scattered the nations. Here people of many languages hear one message.

Peter explains it with the prophet Joel and with the resurrection, and he ends with a claim no one could take back: “God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). About three thousand are baptized. Then Luke shows what they became: people who devoted themselves to teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer, and who shared what they had. Christians differ on whether the baptism of the Spirit is given at conversion or later, and on whether tongues continue today. Both sides read this chapter closely.

open.label: Acts 2, passage by passage
open.why: Wind and fire, the crowd from every nation, Peter's sermon and the life of the first believers, with the question of tongues set out fairly.

also.label: The Holy Spirit
also.why: Short pictures of who the Spirit is, from the breath over the waters at creation to the fire at Pentecost and the life of the church.

also.label: The Holy Spirit
also.why: What the church confesses about the Spirit, with the views on the baptism of the Spirit and the gifts each stated by its own best defenders.

also.label: Do the gifts of the Spirit still happen?
also.why: The case for and against the gifts continuing today, stated fairly, for the question Pentecost raises in every generation.

sessions.question: Of the four things the first believers devoted themselves to, which is most missing from your own life, and why?
sessions.do: Read Acts 2:42-47 slowly and write down every verb. Then choose one of the four things in verse 42 and do it once this week with someone else.

verse.text: They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever been in a crowd where you couldn't understand the language around you? What was it like?
discuss: Peter tells the crowd they crucified the one God made Lord. Why do you think they asked what to do instead of walking away?
Christians differ on the baptism of the Spirit and on tongues. What do the views share, and how can a group hold the difference with charity?
Verses 42 to 47 describe a church that ate together and shared what it had. Which part of that picture is hardest for churches like ours?
group.pray: Give thanks that the good news came to people of every language, and ask in your own words that your church would be devoted to the same four things.

sessions.title: A lame man walks, and a bold church
teaching: At the temple gate called Beautiful, a man who has never walked asks Peter and John for money. Peter has none. He gives him what he has, the name of Jesus, and the man goes into the temple walking and leaping and praising God. Peter refuses the credit: it was not their power or their piety. And he speaks gently to the crowd who handed Jesus over. They acted in ignorance, he says, and the way back is open.

The healing leads to an arrest. Before the same council that condemned Jesus, Peter says there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. The council sees that they are unschooled, ordinary men and recognizes that they had been with Jesus. Told to stop, they say they cannot stop speaking about what they have seen and heard. Then they go home and pray, not for safety, but for boldness, and the place where they meet is shaken.

open.label: Acts 3, passage by passage
open.why: The gate called Beautiful, the name of Jesus, the call to turn back and the prophet like Moses, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Acts 4, passage by passage
also.why: The arrest, no other name, the prayer for boldness and a church of one heart and soul, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Is Jesus the only way?
also.why: Peter's claim of no other name is the hardest sentence in these chapters for many readers, and this answer takes it up honestly.

sessions.question: The council noticed that Peter and John had been with Jesus. What would someone notice about the company you keep?
sessions.do: Read the believers' prayer in Acts 4:24-30 and notice what they ask for and what they don't. Then pray it in your own words for one situation where you are afraid to speak.

verse.text: Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.

care: And if you live with a disability or an illness that has not been healed, this story is not a judgment on your faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who taught you something important without any formal training to do it?
discuss: Peter had no silver or gold. What did he have to give, and what do you have that you could give?
Peter tells the crowd they acted in ignorance. Why do you think he says that, when he has just named what they did?
The believers prayed for boldness rather than safety. Would you have prayed the same prayer? Why or why not?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for anyone in the group who needs courage to speak this week, and for those in the world who are told to stop.

sessions.title: Ananias and Sapphira, and the council
teaching: Chapter 4 ended with Barnabas selling a field and giving the money. Chapter 5 begins with a couple who sell land, keep back part of the price, and pretend to give it all. Peter says plainly that the land was theirs and the money was theirs; the sin was the lie, told to the Holy Spirit. Both die, and great fear falls on the church. It is one of the hardest stories in the New Testament, and it has to be read carefully. It is about a lie at the heart of a new community, not a rule that sudden death today is God's punishment.

Then the apostles are jailed, freed by night, and found teaching in the temple again. Their answer to the high priest has been repeated by Christians under every kind of power since: they must obey God rather than men. A Pharisee named Gamaliel advises caution. If this is of human origin, he says, it will fail, and if it is from God, they cannot stop it. The apostles are flogged and leave rejoicing.

open.label: Acts 5, passage by passage
open.why: Ananias and Sapphira, signs in the streets, the night escape, the answer to the council and Gamaliel's advice, with the hard questions set out plainly.

also.label: Holiness in the whole Bible
also.why: What Scripture means when it calls God holy, from Sinai to the church, so that the fear in this chapter is read in its setting.

also.label: Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes
also.why: Who the high priest's party were, who Gamaliel was, and why the resurrection divided the council that tried the apostles.

sessions.question: Ananias and Sapphira wanted to be seen as more generous than they were. Where are you tempted to look better than you are?
sessions.do: Write down one place where what others see of you is not quite true. Tell God about it plainly, and if it would help, tell one person you trust.

verse.text: But Peter and the other apostles replied, “We must obey God rather than men.”

care: A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is the difference between keeping something private and pretending?
discuss: Peter says the land and the money were theirs to keep. What, then, was the sin?
How should a church hold this story without using it to frighten people or to explain someone's death?
Gamaliel says that what is from God cannot be stopped. Is that a good test? Where might it mislead?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for honesty in your own lives and in your church, and for believers who are told by their rulers to be silent.

sessions.title: Stephen
teaching: Chapter 6 begins with a quarrel. Greek-speaking widows are being overlooked in the daily food, and the apostles ask the church to choose seven men to serve. Every one of the seven has a Greek name. The church answers a complaint from the edge by giving the edge its own leaders. One of them, Stephen, is full of grace and power, and soon he is accused of speaking against the temple and the law.

His defence in chapter 7 is the longest speech in Acts, and it is a retelling of Israel's story: Abraham called outside the land, Joseph rejected by his brothers and raised up, Moses pushed away by the people he came to save. God was never confined to one place, Stephen says, and his people have always resisted the ones he sent. The council is furious. Stephen sees heaven open and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, and he dies praying for those who kill him. A young man named Saul is holding their coats.

open.label: Acts 7, passage by passage
open.why: Stephen's retelling of Abraham, Joseph and Moses, the temple and the tabernacle, and his death, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Acts 6, passage by passage
also.why: The overlooked widows, the seven chosen to serve, and Stephen accused, explained in plain words before his speech.

also.label: Follow a verse
also.why: Stephen's speech is built from Genesis and Exodus. Follow its verses back to where they first stood and see what he chose to tell.

also.label: The age of martyrs
also.why: Stephen was the first of many. The course's lesson on the persecuted church shows what his kind of witness cost in the centuries after.

sessions.question: Stephen died praying for the people killing him. Who is the person you find hardest to pray for, and what would it take to begin?
sessions.do: Read Acts 7:54-60 and then Luke 23:34 and 23:46. Write down every way Stephen's death echoes the death of Jesus, and what that tells you about what Luke wants you to see.

verse.text: While they were stoning him, Stephen appealed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Falling on his knees, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

care: A word for anyone who has lost someone to violence, or who has watched someone they love suffer. Stephen's death is told plainly, and so is his peace. Grief at such a loss is not a lack of faith. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a grief counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Has a complaint ever led to something good in a group you belonged to?
discuss: The church answered the Greek-speaking widows by choosing leaders from among them. What does that say about how a church should hear complaints?
Stephen tells Israel's story as a story of God's people resisting the ones God sent. Why is that story uncomfortable for any church, including ours?
Saul was there, approving. How does knowing what happens to him change the way you read this scene?
group.pray: Give thanks for those who have died faithful, and pray in your own words for the hardest person on your list, as Stephen did.

sessions.title: Philip on the road south
teaching: Stephen's death sets off a persecution, and the believers are scattered, all except the apostles. But the scattering becomes the spreading: those who were driven out preach wherever they go. Philip, another of the seven, goes to Samaria, to the people Jews had kept at a distance for centuries, and they believe. A magician named Simon tries to buy the power to give the Spirit, and Peter refuses him in some of the sharpest words in the book.

Then an angel sends Philip to a desert road, where an official of the queen of the Ethiopians is riding home from Jerusalem, reading Isaiah aloud. He is a eunuch, a man the law kept outside the assembly, and the passage in his hands is about a servant led like a lamb to the slaughter. Philip begins with that very Scripture and tells him about Jesus. When they reach water, the man asks what is to prevent him from being baptized. Nothing does.

open.label: Acts 8, passage by passage
open.why: The scattering, Philip in Samaria, Simon the magician, and the Ethiopian on the desert road with Isaiah 53, each explained in plain words.

also.label: All nations
also.why: Short pictures of God's promise to bless every nation, from Abraham to the crowd in Revelation, the thread this chapter pulls south toward Africa.

also.label: Christianity was never Western
also.why: The faith reached Africa and Asia before it reached most of Europe, and this essay tells that older story the Ethiopian on the road belongs to.

also.label: The Bible atlas
also.why: Find Samaria, Gaza and the road south on the map, and see how far the good news has already travelled from Jerusalem.

sessions.question: The Ethiopian asked what was to prevent him. What do you think keeps people you know from coming near, and is any of it in the church?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 53:7-8, the passage the Ethiopian was reading, then read it again as Philip would have explained it. Write a sentence on what you see now that you didn't before.

verse.text: Then Philip began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.

care: If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who first helped you understand something in the Bible you couldn't understand alone?
discuss: The scattering was a disaster for the church in Jerusalem and the reason the good news spread. How do you hold both of those together?
Simon wanted the Spirit's power without the Spirit's lordship. Where do churches still try to buy what can only be given?
The Ethiopian was a man the law kept outside. Why do you think Luke tells his story at this point in the book?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for someone you know who is reading or searching without help, and ask to be ready to begin where they are.

sessions.title: Saul on the Damascus road
teaching: Saul is on his way to Damascus with letters to arrest anyone belonging to the Way, as the faith was called. A light from heaven drops him to the ground, and a voice asks, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” (Acts 9:4). Notice the last word. To harm the church is to harm Jesus himself. Saul, who thought he was defending God, finds he has been fighting him. He gets up blind and is led by the hand into the city.

The bravest person in the chapter may be Ananias, a believer told to go and lay hands on the man who came to arrest him. He goes, and his first words are “Brother Saul” (Acts 9:17). Later, when the church in Jerusalem is afraid of Saul, Barnabas stands with him. Luke tells this conversion three times in Acts, in chapters 9, 22 and 26, and it is the turn on which the rest of the book hangs.

open.label: Acts 9, passage by passage
open.why: The light on the road, Ananias sent to his enemy, the basket over the wall, Barnabas, and Peter at Lydda and Joppa, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Did Paul invent Christianity?
also.why: The strongest form of the claim that the man converted here made a new religion out of Jesus, and the evidence on the other side.

also.label: How to tell your story
also.why: Paul told his story again and again, before crowds and kings. This guide helps you tell yours plainly, without exaggeration or pressure.

sessions.question: Ananias was asked to welcome the person he most feared. Who would be your Saul, and what would it cost you to call them brother or sister?
sessions.do: Write your own story of coming to faith, or of where you are now, in no more than a page. Then read Acts 22:3-16, Paul's own telling, and notice what he includes.

verse.text: So Ananias went to the house, and when he arrived, he placed his hands on Saul. “Brother Saul,” he said, “the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”

care: If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Has anyone ever surprised you by changing completely?
discuss: Jesus asks why Saul is persecuting him, not his followers. What does that say about how Jesus sees his church?
Ananias and Barnabas both took a risk on Saul. What made their trust different from naivety?
Some people meet God in a single moment and others over years. Why do you think the church has sometimes made Saul's story the only pattern?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for someone you have thought beyond reach, and for the courage of Ananias if God sends you to them.

sessions.title: Peter in a Gentile house, and Peter in prison
teaching: Cornelius is a Roman centurion who fears God and prays. Peter is a Jew who has never eaten anything unclean. God sends each a vision, and Peter's comes three times: a sheet of animals, a command to eat, and a voice saying, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15). Then Peter walks into a Gentile house, a thing his upbringing told him not to do, and while he is still speaking the Spirit falls on everyone listening, before anyone has baptized them. Peter has to explain himself in Jerusalem, and his defence is simple: who was he to hinder God?

In chapter 12 King Herod kills James the brother of John and arrests Peter, meaning to bring him out after the Passover. The church prays earnestly. An angel leads Peter out, and when he knocks at the house where they are praying, they tell the servant girl Rhoda she is out of her mind. The chapter ends with Herod struck down and the word of God spreading.

open.label: Acts 10, passage by passage
open.why: Cornelius, the vision on the roof, Peter in a Gentile house and the Spirit falling before baptism, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Purity and contagion
also.why: Why clean and unclean mattered so much, and why walking into Cornelius's house was harder for Peter than it looks to us.

also.label: Acts 12, passage by passage
also.why: James killed, Peter in chains, Rhoda at the gate and Herod's end, with a note for anyone whose prayer for rescue was not answered.

also.label: The Herods and the governors
also.why: Which Herod this is, how he differs from the Herods of the Gospels, and the rulers Paul will stand before later in the book.

sessions.question: Peter needed a vision three times to cross one line. What line in your own life would take that much for God to move you across?
sessions.do: Read Peter's defence in Acts 11:1-18. Then name one kind of person you would hesitate to eat with, and pray about what Peter learned.

verse.text: Then Peter began to speak: “I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism, but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right.”

care: If you have prayed for someone to be rescued, from illness, from danger, from prison, from death, and the rescue did not come, this chapter does not say your prayer was too weak. The church surely prayed for James too. The three friends in Daniel said God was able to deliver them, “But even if He does not” (Daniel 3:18), they would still trust him. Grief and confusion at such a loss are not a lack of faith. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Was there a kind of person your family taught you, without saying so, to keep at a distance?
discuss: The Spirit fell on Cornelius's house before anyone baptized them. Why do you think God did it in that order, and what did it settle for Peter?
James was killed and Peter was freed, and the church prayed for both. How do you hold those two outcomes together?
The church prayed for Peter and then didn't believe he was at the door. What does that say about the faith God answers?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for those in prison for their faith today, and for any line in your own heart God is asking you to cross.

sessions.title: The first mission
teaching: The church at Antioch, where believers were first called Christians, is worshipping and fasting when the Spirit says to set apart Barnabas and Saul. From here Luke calls Saul by his Roman name, Paul. They sail to Cyprus, then to the cities of what is now southern Turkey. In each city the pattern is the same: Paul goes first to the synagogue and tells Israel's story leading to Jesus, some believe, others are stirred against him, and he moves on.

At Lystra a healing makes the crowd shout that the gods have come down, and they bring bulls to sacrifice. Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes: they are only men. Days later the same city stones Paul and drags him out for dead. He gets up, goes back in, and the next day leaves for Derbe. Then they retrace their steps, appoint elders, and tell the new believers that we must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God.

open.label: Acts 13, passage by passage
open.why: Sent out from Antioch, Cyprus, Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch and the turn to the Gentiles, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Paul's travels
also.why: Follow the first mission on the map, from Antioch to Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe and back.

also.label: Acts 14, passage by passage
also.why: Iconium divided, Lystra's gods, Paul stoned and left for dead, and the long way home, each explained in plain words.

sessions.question: Paul went back into the city that had just stoned him. What makes that courage rather than recklessness?
sessions.do: Open the map of Paul's travels and trace the first mission with your finger. Then read Acts 14:21-28 and write down what they did for the new churches before going home.

verse.text: strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith. “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said.

care: Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever had to go back somewhere that hurt you?
discuss: At Lystra the crowd wanted to worship Paul, and then tried to kill him. What does that say about crowds, and about fame?
Paul tells new believers to expect hardship. Why do you think he said it so early, and do churches today say it?
Paul and Barnabas appointed elders in every church. What does that tell you about what they thought a church needed?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for missionaries and new churches you know of, and for anyone in the group facing a hardship they didn't expect.

sessions.title: The council in Jerusalem
teaching: Some believers from Judea come to Antioch teaching that unless Gentiles are circumcised according to the law of Moses, they cannot be saved. It is a sincere position. The Scriptures commanded circumcision for Abraham's family, and Jesus was a Jew who kept the law. The question was whether Gentiles had to become Jews to belong to Jesus, and it threatened to split the church in two.

So the apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem. Peter tells what happened at Cornelius's house and says we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are. James quotes the prophet Amos and judges that the church should not trouble Gentiles who are turning to God, while asking them to keep a few things that would let Jewish and Gentile believers share a table. Their letter begins, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28). The chapter ends with Paul and Barnabas parting over Mark. A council can settle a doctrine and still not settle a friendship.

open.label: Acts 15, passage by passage
open.why: The dispute over circumcision, Peter and James at the council, the letter to the Gentiles and Paul and Barnabas parting, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The law in the whole Bible
also.why: What God's law was for, from Sinai to the Sermon on the Mount, and how the New Testament speaks of it after Christ.

also.label: Councils and creeds
also.why: The church went on meeting to settle hard questions together, and this lesson follows the councils that gave us the creeds.

also.label: How to disagree without losing the relationship
also.why: Paul and Barnabas parted sharply after the council. This guide is for keeping a friendship through a disagreement that matters.

sessions.question: The believers from Judea were sincere and wrong. What is one thing you have held sincerely that you later had to let go?
sessions.do: Read Acts 15:6-21 and write down, in one sentence each, what Peter, Barnabas and Paul, and James contribute. Notice how each speaks from what God has already done.

verse.text: On the contrary, we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.

group.open: Have you ever been part of a group decision that you thought would split everyone, and didn't?
discuss: Why was the circumcision party's view a serious one, and what would have been lost if the council had agreed with it?
James asked the Gentile believers to keep a few things so that the two groups could eat together. What do we give up today for the sake of a shared table?
Paul and Barnabas agreed on the gospel and still parted over Mark. What do you make of Luke telling us that?
group.pray: Give thanks for the grace that saves Jew and Gentile alike, and pray in your own words for a disagreement in your church or family that needs wisdom.

sessions.title: Philippi and Thessalonica
teaching: A vision of a man of Macedonia calls Paul across the sea, and here the story shifts from they to we: the writer seems to be on the road. At Philippi, a Roman colony, the first believer is Lydia, a businesswoman who sells purple cloth, and her household is baptized. Then Paul frees an enslaved girl from a spirit that made her owners money, and the owners have Paul and Silas beaten and thrown into prison.

At midnight they are singing. An earthquake opens the doors, and the jailer, sure his prisoners have fled, is about to take his own life when Paul calls out that they are all there. The man asks what he must do to be saved, and by morning his household has been baptized and is eating at his table. In Thessalonica the charge against them is telling: they are defying Caesar's decrees, saying there is another king, named Jesus.

open.label: Acts 16, passage by passage
open.why: Timothy, the call to Macedonia, Lydia, the enslaved girl, the midnight prison and the jailer's household, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The gospel against empire
also.why: Words like lord, saviour and good news were already used of the emperor, which is why another king named Jesus sounded like sedition.

also.label: Acts 17, passage by passage
also.why: Thessalonica, Berea and Athens, each explained in plain words; read the first nine verses for this session and keep the rest for the next.

sessions.question: Paul and Silas sang in prison at midnight. What do you think made that possible, and what would make it possible for you?
sessions.do: Make a list of the three households in Acts 16: Lydia, the girl and her owners, the jailer. Write a sentence on what the good news cost or gave each one.

verse.text: They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.”

care: A word of care. Some people come to a moment when everything seems lost, and ending their life seems the only way out. If that is you, please do not carry it alone. Tell God, and tell someone near you: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. If you have thought of ending your life, please reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service where you live. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Paul's first words to the jailer were, ‘Do not harm yourself.’ The night that looked like the end was the night his house was filled with joy.

A word for anyone who has been sold, traded, or forced to work or to do sexual acts by someone who controls them, or who is in that place now. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Which of the people in this chapter would you most like to have met: Lydia, the jailer, or the girl set free?
discuss: The owners turned on Paul when their income was threatened. Where does the good news still cost someone money?
Paul's first words to the jailer were to stop him harming himself. What does that tell you about how the gospel meets a person in despair?
The charge in Thessalonica was that Christians served another king. In what ways is that still true, and in what ways have we made it false?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for anyone who feels at their midnight, and for those still held and used by others for profit.

sessions.title: Athens, Corinth and Ephesus
teaching: In Berea the Jews examine the Scriptures every day to see whether Paul's teaching is true, and Luke calls them noble for it. In Athens Paul is troubled by a city full of idols, and he speaks to the philosophers on the Areopagus. He starts with an altar to an unknown god and quotes their own poets: we are his offspring. He argues that the God who made the world doesn't live in temples, and is not far from any of us. When he reaches the resurrection, some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe.

In Corinth Paul makes tents with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews who had to leave Rome when Claudius expelled them. He stays a year and a half, and the Lord tells him not to be afraid. In Ephesus he teaches for two years, people burn their books of magic, and the silversmiths who make shrines of Artemis start a riot when the good news begins to cost them trade.

open.label: Acts 17, passage by passage
open.why: Berea searching the Scriptures, Athens full of idols, the unknown god and the day of judgment, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The cities of Paul
also.why: What Athens, Corinth and Ephesus were like, and why the good news sounded different in a university town, a port and a temple city.

also.label: Acts 19, passage by passage
also.why: Disciples who knew only John's baptism, the hall of Tyrannus, the books of magic and the riot for Artemis, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Work as worship
also.why: Paul made tents in Corinth while he preached. This guide takes up what it means to see ordinary work as part of a Christian life.

sessions.question: Paul began in Athens with what the Athenians already believed. What does the person you most want to reach already believe that you could begin with?
sessions.do: Read Paul's speech in Acts 17:22-31 aloud. Underline everything he says that a thoughtful person in Athens could agree with, and circle the point where he asks them to go further.

verse.text: God intended that they would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is the best conversation you've had with someone who didn't share your beliefs?
discuss: The Bereans checked Paul against the Scriptures, and Luke praises them. What would it look like for us to read the way they did?
Paul quoted Greek poets in Athens. Where can Christians honestly find common ground with the people around them, and where does it stop?
In Philippi and Ephesus the good news threatened someone's income. What economic idols would it threaten today?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for someone you know who is searching, and for the wisdom to speak to them as Paul spoke in Athens.

sessions.title: Farewell, arrest and the trials
teaching: Paul sets his face toward Jerusalem knowing that prison waits for him. At Miletus he calls the elders of Ephesus and gives them a speech meant for the leaders of a church: keep watch over yourselves and the flock, be shepherds of the church God bought with his own blood, remember that it is more blessed to give than to receive. They weep because they will not see him again. In Jerusalem he is seized in the temple and nearly killed by a mob, and a Roman commander takes him into custody.

Then come the trials: before the crowd, before the council, before the governors Felix and Festus, and before King Agrippa. Felix keeps him two years waiting for a bribe. Paul appeals to Caesar. Each time he tells his story again and comes back to the same point, that he is on trial for the hope of Israel, the resurrection of the dead.

open.label: Acts 20, passage by passage
open.why: Eutychus at the window, the hurry to Jerusalem and Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Acts 26, passage by passage
also.why: Paul before King Agrippa, the third telling of the Damascus road, and Festus calling him mad, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Resurrection in the whole Bible
also.why: Paul says again and again that he is on trial for the resurrection. This study traces that hope from the prophets to the empty tomb.

also.label: The Bible's timeline
also.why: Where Paul's arrest, his two years at Caesarea and his voyage to Rome fall among his letters and the other events of the New Testament.

sessions.question: Paul told his story to crowds, councils, governors and a king, and kept coming back to the resurrection. Why do you think that was the point he would not give up?
sessions.do: Read Acts 20:17-38 as if it were written to the leaders of your own church. Then write a short note of thanks to one of them, naming something specific they have done.

verse.text: Keep watch over yourselves and the entire flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.

care: A word of care. Some people reading this have been kept waiting by a system that is not fair: held without a hearing, a case that drags on for years, a decision put off by people who do not care. This chapter does not tell you that the waiting is good, or that you must be silent about the wrong. Paul spoke up for himself, plainly and with the facts, and Luke names Felix's injustice for what it was. If you are in a long wait like this, you are not forgotten by God. Please do not carry it alone. Share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor, or someone who can give you sound legal advice. If the strain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who is a leader who shepherded you well, and what did they do?
discuss: Paul warned the Ephesian elders that wolves would come from among them. Why might he have said that to the people he trusted most?
Paul used his Roman citizenship and appealed to Caesar. When is it right for a Christian to use the law to protect themselves?
Felix was frightened when Paul spoke of righteousness and judgment, and sent him away until a convenient time. Why do people put off that conversation?
group.pray: Pray in your own words for the leaders of your church by name, and for Christians on trial or waiting in prison anywhere in the world.

sessions.title: Shipwreck, and Rome
teaching: The last two chapters are a sea story, told by someone who seems to have been on board. A prisoner warns the crew not to sail, is overruled, and when a storm has driven them for days and every hope is gone, he stands up among them and tells them to take courage. He takes bread, gives thanks to God in front of them all, and eats. The ship breaks apart off Malta, and every one of the two hundred and seventy-six people aboard reaches land.

Paul reaches Rome in chains, and believers walk out along the Appian Way to meet him. Then Acts simply stops. Paul lives two years in a rented house, welcoming all who come, proclaiming the kingdom of God boldly and without hindrance. We are not told what happened at his trial. Church tradition says he died in Rome, but Luke leaves the book open, as if the story of the witness to the ends of the earth were still being written.

open.label: Acts 27, passage by passage
open.why: The voyage from Caesarea, the storm, Paul's word from the angel, bread broken on the ship and the wreck, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Acts 28, passage by passage
also.why: Malta and the viper, the road to Rome, Paul and the Jewish leaders, and two years in a rented house, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The first Christians
also.why: What happened to the church of Acts after the book stops, from Paul's Rome to the generation after the apostles.

also.label: Deep in one: Romans
also.why: Paul wrote to the church in Rome before he ever reached it. Read next the letter that was waiting for him at the end of Acts.

sessions.question: Acts ends with the story unfinished. What part of it do you think has been handed to you?
sessions.do: Read Acts 28:30-31 and then Acts 1:8 again. Go back to the three circles you drew in the first session and write in the outermost one where you think your own part of the story is.

verse.text: Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him. Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.

care: If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Which of these fourteen sessions will you remember longest, and why?
discuss: In the storm, the prisoner became the one who led. What gave Paul that authority on the ship?
Why might Luke have ended without telling us how Paul's trial turned out?
Looking back over the whole book, what has surprised you most about how the church began?
group.pray: Give thanks for those who carried the good news to you, and pray in your own words for the part of the unfinished story each of you has been given.
